elements.name: Deferred Interrupt Handling
elements.what: Split interrupt servicing into a minimal, fast handler that acknowledges the hardware and a deferred, interruptible context that does the bulk of the work later.
elements.problem: Interrupt handlers run with interrupts masked and cannot sleep; doing real work there increases latency and risks missed interrupts, so the work must be handed off to a schedulable context.
elements.named_in: Linux Kernel Development, 3rd ed. - Robert Love (2010), ch. 'Bottom Halves and Deferring Work'

elements.name: Interrupt Coalescing
elements.what: Hold back events that would each raise an interrupt until a count threshold or timeout is reached, then deliver one interrupt for the whole batch.
elements.problem: Per-event interrupts under high event rates (e.g. NIC packet arrival) swamp the CPU with context switches; batching trades a bounded latency increase for an order-of-magnitude drop in interrupt load. NAPI-style hybrid interrupt/polling is the software realization folded here.
elements.named_in: Interrupt coalescing - Wikipedia (live)

elements.name: Zero-Copy I/O
elements.what: Move data between endpoints (file, socket, device) without copying it through intermediate user-space buffers, via DMA, page remapping, or in-kernel transfer.
elements.problem: Each redundant copy across the user/kernel boundary costs CPU cycles, cache pollution, and memory bandwidth; for high-throughput I/O paths the copies dominate the cost of the transfer itself.
elements.named_in: Zero-copy - Wikipedia

elements.name: Scatter-Gather I/O
elements.what: Perform a single I/O operation over a vector of non-contiguous buffers, scattering input into them or gathering output from them.
elements.problem: Data naturally lives in separate pieces (header + payload, protocol layers); copying it into one contiguous buffer just to do one syscall, or issuing one syscall per piece, both waste work. Also realized in hardware as scatter-gather DMA descriptor chains.
elements.named_in: UNIX Network Programming, Vol. 1 - W. Richard Stevens (1990; 3rd ed. 2003), readv/writev

elements.name: Memory-Mapped File I/O
elements.what: Map a file's contents into the process address space so it is read and written through ordinary memory access, with the OS paging data in and out on demand.
elements.problem: Explicit read/write loops double-buffer data and force the program to manage its own windowing over large files; mapping delegates buffering, caching, and lazy loading to the virtual-memory system and enables sharing between processes. Distinct from memory-mapped device registers (embedded scout's territory).
elements.named_in: Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment - W. Richard Stevens (1992), 'Memory-Mapped I/O'

elements.name: Buddy Memory Allocation
elements.what: Manage memory in power-of-two-sized blocks that split into two 'buddies' on allocation and coalesce back with their buddy on free, found by address arithmetic.
elements.problem: General free-list allocators suffer slow coalescing and external fragmentation; restricting block sizes to powers of two makes split/merge O(1)-ish and bounds fragmentation predictably, at the price of internal fragmentation. Technique due to Knowlton (1965); named and analyzed by Knuth.
elements.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1 - Donald E. Knuth (1968), sec. 2.5 'Dynamic Storage Allocation'

elements.name: Slab Allocator
elements.what: Carve memory into per-type slabs of preconstructed, fixed-size objects and cache freed objects in initialized state for immediate reuse.
elements.problem: Frequently allocated kernel objects pay repeated construction/destruction and fragmentation costs under a general allocator; caching constructed objects per type removes both and improves locality. Slab coloring and the later magazine/vmem layer (Bonwick & Adams 2001) are folded here as variants.
elements.named_in: The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator - Jeff Bonwick (1994)

elements.name: Memory Arena
elements.what: Allocate objects by bumping a pointer through a large block and free them all at once by resetting or discarding the whole arena.
elements.problem: Per-object malloc/free is slow and error-prone when many objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compilation pass); grouping them into one region makes allocation a pointer increment and deallocation a single bulk release. Canonical name decided as 'memory arena' (mission anchor; Hanson's Arena interface); region/bump/linear/frame allocator folded as aka.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996), ch. 'Arenas'

elements.name: Free List
elements.what: Thread freed blocks into a linked list (often stored inside the free blocks themselves) so allocation pops and deallocation pushes in O(1).
elements.problem: An allocator must find reusable blocks without scanning memory; linking free blocks makes recycling constant-time and needs no external metadata. Segregated free lists / size classes folded as the standard variant.
elements.named_in: Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely & Boles (1995)

elements.name: Reference Counting
elements.what: Store with each object a count of live references to it, incremented and decremented as references are created and dropped, reclaiming the object when the count hits zero.
elements.problem: Manual lifetime management fails when ownership is shared and dynamic; counting references reclaims objects deterministically and promptly, at the cost of per-reference bookkeeping and inability to collect cycles unaided.
elements.named_in: A Method for Overlapping and Erasure of Lists - George E. Collins (1960)

elements.name: Weak Reference
elements.what: A reference that does not keep its target alive: it can be dereferenced only while the target still exists and observably lapses when the target is reclaimed.
elements.problem: Reference-counted or traced object graphs with back-pointers, caches, or observer lists otherwise leak via cycles or unwanted retention; a non-owning, lapse-aware reference breaks the cycle while remaining safe to use. Kept as a separate element from reference counting per decision log (distinct mechanism, also exists in tracing-GC runtimes).
elements.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

elements.name: Tracing Garbage Collection
elements.what: Reclaim memory by tracing reachability from a root set and freeing everything not reached, rather than tracking lifetimes at each assignment.
elements.problem: Manual deallocation and pure reference counting are unsafe or incomplete (dangling pointers, cycles); tracing determines liveness globally and correctly. One element by decision: generational, incremental, and concurrent collection are strategy variants folded here, not separate elements.
elements.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

elements.name: Copy-on-Write
elements.what: Share one physical copy of data among logical copies and defer the actual duplication until (and unless) one sharer writes to it.
elements.problem: Eager copying of large state (fork'd address spaces, big strings/containers, snapshots) wastes time and memory when most copies are never modified; write-time copying makes copies O(1) and pays only for actual divergence. Covers both the VM page mechanism and the in-process data-structure idiom; concurrency scout overlap noted.
elements.named_in: Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment - W. Richard Stevens (1992), fork and copy-on-write

elements.name: Self-Pipe Trick
elements.what: A process writes a byte to a pipe it also polls, converting an asynchronous event (typically a signal) into a file-descriptor readiness event handled in the main event loop.
elements.problem: Signals interrupt at arbitrary points and cannot safely do real work, and select/poll cannot wait on them directly; funneling the notification through a self-owned pipe unifies all wakeups race-free in one multiplexing point. Modern kernel equivalents (eventfd, signalfd, pselect) folded here as notes; attributed to D. J. Bernstein.
elements.named_in: The Linux Programming Interface - Michael Kerrisk (2010), sec. 63.5.2 'The Self-Pipe Trick'

elements.name: Sliding Window Flow Control
elements.what: Sender and receiver agree on a window of unacknowledged data that may be in flight; acknowledgments slide the window forward, throttling the sender to the receiver's capacity.
elements.problem: Stop-and-wait wastes bandwidth on every round trip, while unlimited sending overruns the receiver; a sliding window pipelines transmission up to a negotiated bound and doubles as the receiver's backpressure signal. Go-back-N and selective repeat are retransmission variants folded here; silly-window-syndrome avoidance noted.
elements.named_in: TCP/IP Illustrated, Vol. 1: The Protocols - W. Richard Stevens (1994)

elements.name: Nagle's Algorithm
elements.what: Coalesce small outgoing writes by holding new small segments while any previously sent data remains unacknowledged, sending them as one larger segment when the ACK arrives.
elements.problem: Streams of tiny writes (keystrokes, RPC headers) generate one mostly-header packet each, congesting the network; self-clocked coalescing amortizes header overhead without a fixed timer. Interaction with delayed ACK and the TCP_CORK variant noted.
elements.named_in: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks - John Nagle (1984)
elements.borderline: Stack-internal in TCP, but the small-write-coalescing mechanism is named, recurring, and reimplemented in user protocol libraries - kept IN.

elements.name: Jitter Buffer
elements.what: Buffer arriving media packets briefly and release them on a steady clock (reordering by sequence number), absorbing variation in network transit time.
elements.problem: Real-time audio/video must be played at a constant rate but packets arrive with variable delay and out of order; buffering trades a bounded added latency for smooth, gap-free playout. Static vs adaptive sizing folded as variants.
elements.named_in: Understanding Jitter in Packet Voice Networks - Cisco (live technical doc)

elements.name: Heartbeat
elements.what: Periodically send a small liveness message (or probe an idle peer) so that silence beyond a threshold reveals a dead, hung, or unreachable counterpart.
elements.problem: A failed peer or severed connection is otherwise indistinguishable from one that is merely idle; periodic signals bound failure-detection time and let half-open connections be reaped. Keepalive (RFC 1122 TCP keepalive) folded as aka per decision log. Same-name architecture-realm tactic (Bass availability 'heartbeat') exists - bridge in Phase 3, do not collapse.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Robert S. Hanmer (2007), 'Heartbeat'

elements.name: Guard Page
elements.what: Place an inaccessible (or trap-on-touch) memory page or poisoned band adjacent to a stack or allocation so that overrun/overflow faults immediately at the boundary instead of corrupting neighbors.
elements.problem: Buffer and stack overflows silently corrupt adjacent memory and surface far from the bug; a trapping boundary converts the overrun into an immediate, located fault (and enables lazy stack growth). Allocator redzones (ASan-style poisoned bands) folded as aka; distinct from the ABI 'red zone' stack optimization.
elements.named_in: Creating Guard Pages - Microsoft Win32 documentation (live)
elements.borderline: Relies on MMU protection, so it straddles the OS/hardware boundary - but it is set up inside one program (allocator, runtime, thread library), so kept IN.

elements.name: Stack Canary
elements.what: Write a known guard value between a stack frame's buffers and its control data and verify it before returning; a changed canary means the frame was overflowed.
elements.problem: Stack buffer overflows overwrite return addresses and enable control-flow hijack; a checked sentinel detects the overwrite before the corrupted return address is used, aborting instead of being exploited.
elements.named_in: StackGuard: Automatic Adaptive Detection and Prevention of Buffer-Overflow Attacks - Cowan et al. (1998)

elements.name: Token Bucket
elements.what: Accumulate tokens into a bucket at a fixed rate up to a burst capacity; each action consumes tokens and is delayed or rejected when the bucket is empty.
elements.problem: Rate limiting must bound average throughput while still absorbing legitimate bursts; a replenishing token budget enforces the long-term rate with a tunable burst allowance, in a few integers of state.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks - Andrew S. Tanenbaum (1981; 5th ed. 2011), traffic shaping

elements.name: Leaky Bucket
elements.what: Queue arriving items in a fixed-capacity bucket that drains at a constant rate, emitting a perfectly smoothed output stream and dropping arrivals that overflow.
elements.problem: Bursty producers must sometimes be forced to a strictly constant output rate (traffic shaping, pacing); a constant-drain queue enforces the rate exactly, unlike token bucket which permits bursts. Kept separate from token bucket per decision log: the mechanisms and output behaviors genuinely differ. Named by J. S. Turner (1986).
elements.named_in: Computer Networks - Andrew S. Tanenbaum (1981; 5th ed. 2011), traffic shaping

elements.name: Byte Stuffing
elements.what: Mark frame boundaries with a reserved delimiter byte and escape occurrences of that byte (and the escape itself) inside the payload so the delimiter is unambiguous.
elements.problem: A byte stream has no inherent message boundaries and payloads may contain any byte value; stuffing lets a receiver resynchronize on delimiters regardless of payload content. Bit stuffing (HDLC) and COBS (Cheshire & Baker 1997) folded as variants; length-prefix/TLV framing left to the serialization scout.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks - Andrew S. Tanenbaum (1981; 5th ed. 2011), framing

elements.name: Happy Eyeballs
elements.what: Race connection attempts over alternative paths (canonically IPv6 vs IPv4) with small staggered delays, keep the first to succeed, and cancel the rest.
elements.problem: Trying alternatives strictly in sequence makes users wait out full timeouts when the preferred path is broken; staggered parallel attempts hide failures at the cost of a little duplicate work.
elements.named_in: RFC 8305: Happy Eyeballs Version 2: Better Connectivity Using Concurrency - Schinazi & Pauly (2017)

parked_architecture.name: Server concurrency models (iterative, process-per-connection, preforked, prethreaded server)
parked_architecture.why: Stevens UNP ch. 30 catalogs these as whole-server structural alternatives - system-level structure, not an in-component mechanism; feed Phase 3 (relates to thread pool, Leader/Followers).

parked_architecture.name: Kernel-bypass networking (DPDK, user-space network stacks)
parked_architecture.why: A restructuring of the whole I/O path across OS/application boundary - deployment/system-structure decision, not implementable inside one component.

parked_architecture.name: Split top-half/bottom-half driver architecture (as OS structuring principle)
parked_architecture.why: The per-driver mechanism is IN as deferred-interrupt-handling; the kernel-wide layering of all drivers into halves is a statement of system structure for Phase 3.

excluded_notable.name: Pipes / FIFOs (OS IPC facility)
excluded_notable.why: Kernel-provided facility, not an implementable element; the in-process analog (inter-thread channel / blocking queue) is the communication scout's element.

excluded_notable.name: Shared memory segments (System V / POSIX shm)
excluded_notable.why: Facility-not-element; in-process analog is plain shared address-space state plus synchronization primitives (concurrency scout).

excluded_notable.name: System V / POSIX message queues, UNIX domain sockets
excluded_notable.why: OS facilities; the design-level element is the in-process message queue / mailbox (communication scout).

excluded_notable.name: Readiness- vs completion-based I/O multiplexing (select/poll/epoll/kqueue vs IOCP/io_uring)
excluded_notable.why: The syscall families are facilities; the design-level elements are Reactor and Proactor, owned by POSA2 (corpus id posa2) via the concurrency scout.

excluded_notable.name: Page-replacement policies (LRU, clock, second-chance, WSClock)
excluded_notable.why: OS instance of cache eviction - fold as a note under the cache-eviction-policy element (caching scout owns); policy variants are the algorithmics zoo.

excluded_notable.name: TCP congestion-control algorithm family (slow start, AIMD, CUBIC, BBR)
excluded_notable.why: Stack-internal algorithm zoo, not a reusable in-process building block; AIMD as a concept may merit a note under rate limiting if another scout claims it.

excluded_notable.name: Demand paging / virtual memory
excluded_notable.why: OS facility spanning hardware and kernel; the in-process analog is lazy loading / lazy initialization (creational scout).

excluded_notable.name: ASLR (address space layout randomization)
excluded_notable.why: OS loader/kernel security facility, not implementable inside one program.

excluded_notable.name: UNIX signals (as a facility)
excluded_notable.why: Kernel-delivered asynchronous notification facility; the design-level handling idiom is captured as the self-pipe trick element.

excluded_notable.name: Active queue management (RED, CoDel)
excluded_notable.why: Network-infrastructure queue policy running in routers; algorithm family rather than an in-process design element.

notes: Decision log: (1) region/arena/bump allocator collapsed into ONE element 'memory-arena' - canonical name follows the mission anchor and Hanson's Arenas chapter (corpus id hanson); region-based memory management (Tofte-Talpin), bump/linear/frame allocator, obstack all aka. (2) Weak reference kept as a SEPARATE element from reference counting: distinct mechanism, also meaningful under tracing GC. (3) Tracing GC is one element; generational/incremental/concurrent/copying are folded variants. (4) Keepalive folded into heartbeat aka (Hanmer's Heartbeat pattern, corpus id hanmer); same-name architecture tactic (Bass) flagged for the Phase 3 same-name-two-realms rule. (5) NAPI hybrid interrupt/polling folded into interrupt-coalescing. (6) sendfile/splice folded into zero-copy; eventfd/signalfd folded into self-pipe trick as modern replacements; go-back-N/selective-repeat folded into sliding window; slab coloring and magazines folded into slab allocator; delayed-ACK interaction and TCP_CORK noted under Nagle. (7) Token bucket and leaky bucket kept as two elements (genuinely different output behavior: bursts allowed vs strict smoothing). (8) Guard page and stack canary kept as two elements (page-protection trap vs checked sentinel value). Overlap flags for merge: deferred-interrupt-handling (embedded scout), copy-on-write (concurrency scout), token-bucket rate limiting (robustness scout), byte-stuffing/COBS (embedded scout may also surface it), stack-canary (security scout if one exists). Deliberately left to other scouts: timer wheel (scheduling), RCU/hazard pointers/seqlock (concurrency), circular/ring buffer and backpressure (data-flow), checksums/CRC (embedded or robustness), TLV/length-prefix framing (serialization), connection pool (resource, via object pool). Confidence: 21 established, 3 spot-checked (interrupt coalescing via Wikipedia article, guard page via Microsoft Win32 'Creating Guard Pages' doc, jitter buffer via Cisco 'Understanding Jitter in Packet Voice Networks' doc - all confirmed live this session).
